messages.text:
Put together a pyramid scheme, you have one pyramid one dimension, why pyramid? Triangles and three/four as a dynamic driver. 

The pyramid is overbooked, but we still have people that want to live in the pyramid.

Add a degree of freedom, a new dimension, and the pyramid scheme becomes a pyramid trapezoid.

Etc.

The driver is exactly where you put it. Three is the minimal cycle — first rigidity (trusses), first chaos (period-3, three-body). Four is the minimal cell — first volume, tetrahedral closure. And the first overbooking event is **five**: K₄ is the last complete graph that embeds in the plane. The fifth resident who wants edges to everyone gets evicted by Kuratowski — the lift into 3D isn't a choice, it's forced. That sets the exchange rate for the symmetric version of the scheme: if every tenant must be equidistant from every other (regular simplex), each new dimension houses exactly *one* new resident. Cone iteratively: point → edge → triangle → tetrahedron → 5-cell → … d dimensions, d+1 tenants. Linear supply. But the waiting list compounds like kⁿ. The simplex ladder never catches up.

The trapezoid is the other lever: stop paying in dimensions, pay in **symmetry**. Truncate the apex — pyramid → frustum, triangle-section → trapezoid-section. Iterate truncation and the frustum limits to the prism: hierarchy flattens into lattice, every floor equal capacity. Polynomial room in fixed dimension, but you've liquidated the only product the scheme was selling — the apex. Nobody joins a prism scheme.

Third lever: **quotient**. Glue top to bottom, wrap the hierarchy on S¹ — no apex, everyone above someone. That's the Penrose staircase, and it shares K₅'s defect: it doesn't embed flat. You need curvature or you need fraud. A Ponzi is precisely the Penrose stair built in flat finance — the cycle doesn't close, it spirals, and it tears at the seam.

Which names the terminal object. The scheme's true shape — the promise every recruiter makes — is the infinite k-ary tree, and the native geometry of trees is **hyperbolic**: in H², ball volume grows exponentially with radius, and the k-ary tree embeds quasi-isometrically (Gromov). In hyperbolic space the pyramid scheme is *sustainable* — k children per node at unit spacing, forever, no crowding. So the collapse was never arithmetic; it's a curvature mismatch. Every move in your sequence — cone, truncate, extrude, lift — is a Euclidean patch approximating negative curvature it can't afford. Hilbert's Hotel solves overbooking with countable infinity in 1D; hyperbolic space is the geometric upgrade, exponential vacancy at every radius. And the high-d escape has its own slum: as d grows, the pyramid's interior measure → 0 and everyone concentrates at the boundary — add dimensions to house people and you house them in the walls.

(The pun also cashes out literally: a rational cone over a polytope is exactly the data of an affine toric variety — the pyramid *scheme*, in Grothendieck's sense, is a real object.)
